headline: Maine begins automatic electric-bill discounts for eligible low-income households
dek: A new SupportLink process will connect existing benefit records to Maine's electric-assistance program, with monthly discounts for eligible CMP and Versant customers.
body: Maine has begun automatically enrolling eligible low-income households in a redesigned electric-bill assistance program, a change intended to reach people who qualified for help but never completed a separate utility application. The Mills administration said the new process began Oct. 1 through SupportLink, an initiative that connects information from existing public-benefit programs with other services. The governor's announcement is available from the [Office of Gov. Janet Mills](https://www.maine.gov/governor/mills/news/governor-mills-announces-automatic-electric-bill-discounts-thousands-maine-families-2026-10-01).

The assistance comes through Maine's Low Income Assistance Program, or LIAP. The state Department of Health and Human Services will use records from programs including the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, Temporary Assistance for Needy Families and MaineCare to identify households that may qualify. The information is shared with participating utilities so a qualifying customer can receive the benefit without separately sending the same eligibility documents to the utility, according to the governor's office. The program is designed with an opt-out option rather than requiring every household to begin with a new application.

The change could affect a large group of Mainers. State officials said about 44,000 ratepayers participated in LIAP last year, while DHHS had identified roughly 67,000 households as eligible. That gap is the practical problem the automatic-enrollment system is meant to address: a household may qualify for assistance through another program but still miss a utility deadline, overlook a notice or lack the time to assemble paperwork. Maine Public's [report on the rollout](https://www.mainepublic.org/business-and-economy/2026-10-01/low-income-mainers-auto-enrolled-for-electric-discounts) said the department expects tens of thousands of additional households to enter the program because of the change.

For customers of Central Maine Power, the monthly discount will vary by income and can range from 25% to 81% of the bill, the governor's office said. Versant customers can receive between 17% and 83%. Those percentages are not a universal reduction for every low-income customer: the amount depends on the household's eligibility and the utility serving it. The benefit is also a discount on the electric bill, not a payment that can be used for heating oil, propane, rent or other household expenses.

The redesigned program changes when customers see the assistance. In previous years, LIAP money was applied as a lump-sum credit, which could leave a participant facing a larger bill after the credit was used up. For eligible CMP and Versant customers, the benefit will now be applied as a monthly percentage discount. The state's Office of the Public Advocate explains that qualifying customers served by smaller consumer-owned utilities will continue to receive LIAP assistance as lump-sum credits; its [electricity program update](https://www.maine.gov/meopa/electricity/WWWO) describes the distinction.

The Mills administration said about $40 million is available for the electric discounts and related assistance this year. Maine Public reported that the total funding is roughly $40.5 million and that the program's financing includes state funds, a surcharge on utility bills and money associated with the New England Clean Energy Connect transmission project. Those funding figures describe the program as a whole, not an amount reserved for each household, and the discount structure means the value of an individual benefit depends on the customer's bill and eligibility tier.

Automatic enrollment does not mean every household with a low income will see a credit on every type of electric bill. The program is tied to participating utilities and to eligibility rules: a household generally must have income at or below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines or qualify for the federally funded Home Energy Assistance Program, according to the governor's announcement. A customer whose records do not match may still need to apply or provide documentation. People who do not want their information used for the match can opt out, and customers with questions should contact their utility or Maine's public-benefit assistance network rather than assume that a missing credit means they are ineligible.

The rollout arrives as Maine households face higher energy costs and as the state also directs residents toward separate heating assistance. LIAP is focused on electricity bills; the Home Energy Assistance Program, or HEAP, helps eligible renters and homeowners pay for heating fuel and electric heat through local Community Action Agencies. The two programs can overlap for an eligible household, but one does not replace the other. Maine's [Office of the Public Advocate income-qualified resources](https://www.maine.gov/meopa/consumer-resources/income-qualified-resources) lists the programs and notes that LIAP is changing in October 2026.

The near-term test for SupportLink is whether the new data connection converts eligibility into reliable help before winter bills arrive. The state has announced the rules and participating utility process, but households still need to read their bills and notices, protect their account information and seek assistance if the expected discount does not appear. The automatic system removes one paperwork barrier; it does not remove the need to confirm that a household's income, benefit status, utility account and address are correctly recorded.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Maine begins automatic LIAP electric-bill discounts
seoDescription: Maine's SupportLink system is automatically enrolling eligible low-income households in monthly electric-bill discounts through LIAP.
